en.location: 📍 Hamlet of Halle-Heide near Halle (municipality of Oost Gelre), towards Mariënvelde · freely accessible; a 13 km circuit starts at the Halle-Heideweg
en.description: The Hallse Heide features on the terrain list of Staatsbosbeheer as a sub-area of its Achterhoek nature area and also lives on in the name of the hamlet Halle-Heide between Halle and Mariënvelde. The “heath” here is mostly history: the extensive heathland of the old common of Halle was reclaimed in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries into open pasture and arable land, interspersed with woods, shelterbelts and hedgerows. The Staatsbosbeheer terrain has no visitor page of its own; to experience the area, walk the robust 13-kilometre circuit that starts in the hamlet and leads via quiet roads, sandy tracks and well-kept church paths to Mariënvelde. en.description: The Reirinkbos is a wood of Het Geldersch Landschap of about 10 hectares, acquired in 1973 and situated just outside Groenlo in the municipality of Oost Gelre — the wooded part of the former Reirink estate, which further consists of farmland and an old farmstead. In the wood, mixed forest, alder coppice, nature grassland patches, a small fen and pools alternate: precisely the small-scale Achterhoek pattern that largely disappeared in the surroundings when the hedgerows around farms and parcels were removed. Botanically striking are wild bog-myrtle and hard fern, old-wood indicators such as wood anemone, common Solomon’s seal and wood sorrel, and in the wet grasslands water ragwort and ragged-robin. Many birds breed here, including the spotted flycatcher, and the white admiral flies along the forest edges. History lies beneath the forest floor: part of the Reirinkbos is an archaeological monument — the wood lies partly on the site of the former army camp of Count Ernst Casimir in the circumvallation line of Groenlo, the 15-kilometre siege rampart with moat built around the town in 1627.

1939Reirinkbos

📍 Just outside Groenlo (municipality of Oost Gelre), in the small-scale land between the town and Lievelde · freely accessible on the paths

The Reirinkbos is a wood of Het Geldersch Landschap of about 10 hectares, acquired in 1973 and situated just outside Groenlo in the municipality of Oost Gelre — the wooded part of the former Reirink estate, which further consists of farmland and an old farmstead. In the wood, mixed forest, alder coppice, nature grassland patches, a small fen and pools alternate: precisely the small-scale Achterhoek pattern that largely disappeared in the surroundings when the hedgerows around farms and parcels were removed. Botanically striking are wild bog-myrtle and hard fern, old-wood indicators such as wood anemone, common Solomon’s seal and wood sorrel, and in the wet grasslands water ragwort and ragged-robin. Many birds breed here, including the spotted flycatcher, and the white admiral flies along the forest edges. History lies beneath the forest floor: part of the Reirinkbos is an archaeological monument — the wood lies partly on the site of the former army camp of Count Ernst Casimir in the circumvallation line of Groenlo, the 15-kilometre siege rampart with moat built around the town in 1627.

nl.description: Het Meddoscheveld — ook wel Meddose Veld genoemd — is het open veld- en ontginningslandschap rond de buurtschap Meddo, ten noorden van Winterswijk. en.description: The Vragenderveld is the open field around the village of Vragender, between the Winterswijk–Zutphen railway line and the valley of the Visserijbeek: one of the large-scale, wet heath reclamations that lie south-west of the Groenlose Slinge and were turned from heath and peat into arable and pasture land in the twentieth century. en.description: Het Waliën is the name of one of the oldest manor houses of the Winterswijk area, situated in the hamlet of Huppel on the Waliënseweg. In 1570 the “huis Walyen” appears for the first time, alongside farms such as Keylwinck, Bennekinck and Boevekinck; it concerned a non-recognised manor with building and pasture land, moated and surrounded by gardens, orchards and farmyards. After a fire in 1759 the house fell into decay; in July 1908 the estate was auctioned and fell apart: the ten farms and all the land were sold, the municipality bought ground for a school and the ruin with kitchen garden and a piece of wood came into the hands of textile manufacturer Willem Willink. What remains is a ruin whose wall with chimney frieze has been a national monument since 2011, parts of the old moat and some outbuildings — visible from the public road. Het Waliën is not an accessible nature terrain, but it is a striking cultural-historical walking destination on the edge of the Nationaal Landschap Winterswijk, combinable with the nature areas Bönnink and Dottinkrade in the same surroundings.

1946Het Waliën

📍 Waliënseweg near Winterswijk (hamlet of Huppel) · the ruin lies along the public road and can be viewed from there; no car park or paths of its own

Het Waliën is the name of one of the oldest manor houses of the Winterswijk area, situated in the hamlet of Huppel on the Waliënseweg. In 1570 the “huis Walyen” appears for the first time, alongside farms such as Keylwinck, Bennekinck and Boevekinck; it concerned a non-recognised manor with building and pasture land, moated and surrounded by gardens, orchards and farmyards. After a fire in 1759 the house fell into decay; in July 1908 the estate was auctioned and fell apart: the ten farms and all the land were sold, the municipality bought ground for a school and the ruin with kitchen garden and a piece of wood came into the hands of textile manufacturer Willem Willink. What remains is a ruin whose wall with chimney frieze has been a national monument since 2011, parts of the old moat and some outbuildings — visible from the public road. Het Waliën is not an accessible nature terrain, but it is a striking cultural-historical walking destination on the edge of the Nationaal Landschap Winterswijk, combinable with the nature areas Bönnink and Dottinkrade in the same surroundings.

nl.description: Het Rutbeek is een recreatie- en natuurpark van circa 120 hectare aan de zuidkant van Enschede, ontstaan door grootschalige zandwinning: in de jaren zeventig werd hier zand gewonnen voor de wegen en wijken van Enschede, waarna het gat volliep met water. In 1975 werd begonnen met de aanleg van het recreatiegebied; in 1978 ging het eerste deel open en in 1982 was het park voltooid. Rond de grote plas liggen stranden, rietkragen, bospercelen, moerasjes en graslanden, met hoogteverschillen die door de zandwinning zijn ontstaan; het water is afgeschermd zwemwater, en op en om de plas wordt gezwommen, gezeild, gesurft, gereden (waterski) en gevist. Het park heeft ook natuurwaarde: in de bossen groeien onder meer wilde gagel en diverse orchideeën, de schone vijvers herbergen kranswieren en kleine natuurgebiedjes dienen als thuisbasis voor de beschermde zandhagedis. Bijzonder is de archeologische belevingsplek “Laag van Usselo” aan de rand van de plas, waar rendierjagers uit de steentijd hun sporen achterlieten. Rond het water lopen gemarkeerde wandelroutes door een verrassend afwisselend landschap van bos, vennen en open grasland.

nl.description: Landgoed Groot Brunink ligt aan de zuidkant van Enschede, ingebed in het Twentse hoevelandschap tussen de stad en het buitengebied. De geschiedenis gaat terug tot 1341, toen de Hof te Brunink een borgleen was van de Nijeborg en daarmee indirect onder de bisschop van Münster viel; restanten van gracht, hoesstee en de zogenaamde Heerenwal herinneren nog aan die tijd. Het landgoed is circa 100 hectare groot en bestaat uit loof- en naaldbossen, houtwallen, weilanden en akkers, doorsneden door de Bruninksbeek; sinds 2013 beheert Landschap Overijssel een deel van circa 27 hectare (erfpacht van de gemeente Enschede), terwijl de monumentale boerderij Hof Brunink — een rijksmonument met jaarankers uit 1849 — tegenwoordig een biologisch melkveebedrijf huisvest. Het landgoed is een paradijs voor vogels met zo’n 58 soorten, waaronder bosuil, patrijs en diverse spechten, en ree en vos laten er regelmatig hun sporen achter. Over het landgoed lopen wandelroutes van Landschap Overijssel en het IVN, die ook de mysterieuze put op Erve Brunink aandoen waarover verschillende verhalen de ronde doen.

en.description: The Groot Brunink estate lies on the south side of Enschede, embedded in the Twente farm landscape between the city and the countryside. The history goes back to 1341, when the Hof te Brunink was a fief of the Nijeborg and thus indirectly under the bishop of Münster; remnants of moat, farmstead and the so-called Heerenwal still recall that era. The estate covers about 100 hectares and consists of broadleaf and conifer woods, hedgerows, pastures and fields, intersected by the Bruninksbeek; since 2013 Landschap Overijssel manages a part of about 27 hectares (leasehold from the municipality of Enschede), while the monumental farmstead Hof Brunink — a national monument with anchor dates from 1849 — now houses an organic dairy farm. The estate is a paradise for birds with some 58 species, including tawny owl, partridge and several woodpeckers, and roe deer and fox regularly leave their traces here. Walking routes of Landschap Overijssel and IVN run over the estate, also passing the mysterious well on Erve Brunink about which various stories circulate.

Landgoed Groot Brunink ligt aan de zuidkant van Enschede, ingebed in het Twentse hoevelandschap tussen de stad en het buitengebied. De geschiedenis gaat terug tot 1341, toen de Hof te Brunink een borgleen was van de Nijeborg en daarmee indirect onder de bisschop van Münster viel; restanten van gracht, hoesstee en de zogenaamde Heerenwal herinneren nog aan die tijd. Over het landgoed lopen wandelroutes van Landschap Overijssel en het IVN, die ook de mysterieuze put op Erve Brunink aandoen waarover verschillende verhalen de ronde doen.

1951Groot Brunink

📍 On the south side of Enschede, between Usselo and the Lonneker countryside · freely accessible over roads and paths; walking routes start at the entrance avenue on the Bruninkslaan

The Groot Brunink estate lies on the south side of Enschede, embedded in the Twente farm landscape between the city and the countryside. The history goes back to 1341, when the Hof te Brunink was a fief of the Nijeborg and thus indirectly under the bishop of Münster; remnants of moat, farmstead and the so-called Heerenwal still recall that era. The estate covers about 100 hectares and consists of broadleaf and conifer woods, hedgerows, pastures and fields, intersected by the Bruninksbeek; since 2013 Landschap Overijssel manages a part of about 27 hectares (leasehold from the municipality of Enschede), while the monumental farmstead Hof Brunink — a national monument with anchor dates from 1849 — now houses an organic dairy farm. The estate is a paradise for birds with some 58 species, including tawny owl, partridge and several woodpeckers, and roe deer and fox regularly leave their traces here. Walking routes of Landschap Overijssel and IVN run over the estate, also passing the mysterious well on Erve Brunink about which various stories circulate.

en.location: 📍 South-east of Enschede, against the German border · freely accessible on roads and paths; car park at the Aamsveenweg/Sagenweg, excursions start at Huize Hölterhof
en.description: The Aamsveen is one of the last living raised-bog areas of the Netherlands, situated south-east of Enschede on the border with Germany, where it continues into the much larger Amtsvenn-Hündfelder Moor. The Dutch part is managed by Landschap Overijssel and has been designated a Natura 2000 area. The bog arose after the cutting of large stretches of raised bog: you will find cut-over bog with peat pits, wet fen woods, heath fields and species-poor grasslands, intersected by the Glanerbeek. Of the roughly one hundred hectares of living raised bog that remain in the Netherlands, more than a tenth lies in the Aamsveen. A fire in 2011 burnt a large part of the area to ashes; since then Landschap Overijssel works with German partners on cross-border raised-bog restoration — with dams, weirs and sealing, the water level is stabilised so that new sphagnum moss can grow. The interior of the bog is partly closed during the restoration works; walkers follow the paths on the edge, and those who want to enter the bog can join the excursions of Landschap Overijssel and the Biologisches Station Zwillbrock.

1953Aamsveen

📍 South-east of Enschede, against the German border · freely accessible on roads and paths; car park at the Aamsveenweg/Sagenweg, excursions start at Huize Hölterhof

The Aamsveen is one of the last living raised-bog areas of the Netherlands, situated south-east of Enschede on the border with Germany, where it continues into the much larger Amtsvenn-Hündfelder Moor. The Dutch part is managed by Landschap Overijssel and has been designated a Natura 2000 area. The bog arose after the cutting of large stretches of raised bog: you will find cut-over bog with peat pits, wet fen woods, heath fields and species-poor grasslands, intersected by the Glanerbeek. Of the roughly one hundred hectares of living raised bog that remain in the Netherlands, more than a tenth lies in the Aamsveen. A fire in 2011 burnt a large part of the area to ashes; since then Landschap Overijssel works with German partners on cross-border raised-bog restoration — with dams, weirs and sealing, the water level is stabilised so that new sphagnum moss can grow. The interior of the bog is partly closed during the restoration works; walkers follow the paths on the edge, and those who want to enter the bog can join the excursions of Landschap Overijssel and the Biologisches Station Zwillbrock.

Best season & peak months: Apr–Oct, May–Jun (birdsong and dragonflies), Sep (heath in bloom)
Best time of day: Early morning — peace and mist above the bog.
